newsitem.title: USA: Soybeans, corn rise on weather, silver also gains.
newsitem.headline: Soybeans, corn rise on weather, silver also gains.

text.p: Soybean prices rose strongly on Thursday on reports of strong export demand and forecasts for more dry weather in the Midwest as soybeans head into a key stage of growth.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for post-harvest delivery in November rose 24-1/4 cents a bushel to close at $6.58. Corn was buoyed by the rally, with December corn ending up 4-1/4 cents a bushel at $2.67-3/4.

"The outlook is drier for next week," said Mario Balletto, oilseeds analyst with Merrill Lynch. "The crop needs more rain, and not enough rain is being forecast right now. The anticipation of yield losses is starting to develop."

Soybeans were boosted from the opening by a weekly report showing strong exports. The U.S. Agriculture Department said net sales of soybeans for the current 1996/97 year in the week ended July 24 were 125,300 metric tons, above trader expectations for 50,000 to 100,000 tons.
Corn prices were aided by the dry weather concerns.

"There appears to be no significant rain for the dry areas of central and southern Illinois, parts of central and southwestern Indiana, eastern Missouri and eastern Iowa for the next seven to ten days," said Weather Services Corp meteorologist Mike Palmerino.
"This weather will continue to raise concerns about this year's corn production in those states," he said.
In New York, silver prices rose on positive sentiment about future demand from jewelers and other fabricators, helping the metal buck fresh negative sentiment about gold.
Silver for September delivery at the COMEX closed 11.7 cents higher at $4.490 an ounce, breaking out of the range of $4.20-4.40 seen for the past three weeks.

"We continue to feel that downside potential for the nearby futures will be limited by another global supply deficit and continued good import demand from the U.S., Japan and India," said Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer.
U.S. silver imports rose 12 percent in the January-April period this year to 547 metric tons, while Japanese silver imports rose 33 percent from January to May to 602 tons.
By contrast, worries about further central bank gold sales surfaced again on Thursday to renew pressure on the market.
December gold fell $2.00 an ounce to close at $328.60.
The central bank of Lithuania said it was considering selling some of its gold reserves in the future, although Lithuania held only $62.1 million of gold reserves as of June.
Following heavy sales in recent months by Australian and European central banks, however, the talk weighed on prices.
"Further price weakness in expected for the gold market in the third quarter, with the seasonal slowdown in fabrication demand adding to already very negative market sentiment," Rinehimer said.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, pork belly prices rose strongly for a second straight day on indications that meat shipments to Japan will pick up again next month when a tariff is dropped on pork imports.
Pork bellies for August delivery closed up the allowable 3.00 cent a pound daily trading limit at 86.200 cents.

"It looks like the packers intend to keep their market share so they continue to be underneath the market giving us some support on the cash and the futures," said Don Roose, President of U.S. Commodities Inc.

Japan has said it will drop its tariff on imported pork in August to help bring down pork prices for Japanese consumers. Speculation has circulated in the market this week that Japan my extend that move beyond August.
"Their inventory ran low and they are trying to replenish and they are going to replenish the easiest way they can," Roose said of Japan's pork inventories.
Oil prices fell back at the New York Mercantile Exchnage in largely technical trade ahead of the expiration of the August gasoline contract on Thursday.
August gasoline, which had risen sharply this week on worries about tight cash market supplies, settled at 67.84 cents, down 2.06 cents.
"Traders with short positions finished getting out yesterday leaving the speculators who were long to fend for themselves and leave today," said analyst Tim Evans at Pegasus Econometric Group.
Tracking gasoline, September crude ended 16 cents a barrel lower at $20.14 while August heating oil ended 0.17 cent off at 55.61 cents a gallon.
